À un clic, à un contact, à un contrat :: One click, one contact, one contract: How teenagers are being pulled into crime
À Montréal, des adolescents sont recruté: In Montréal, teenagers are being recruited for criminal “contracts” through social media, and the consequences are often tragic.
À Montréal, des adolescents reçoivent de: In Montréal, teenagers receive criminal “contracts” by phone. Illustration: Sonia Ekiyor-Katimi
Ce reportage fait état du recrutement de: This report looks at how young people, including minors, are being recruited by criminal networks in Montréal to carry out “jobs”: thefts, arson, acts of intimidation. It is a reality that is increasingly visible in public space, but whose mechanisms are not all well understood, particularly when recruitment happens through close circles or social media.
Cet article s’appuie sur les témoignages: This article draws on the raw testimonies of young people who have experienced, up close or from a distance, being recruited to carry out contracts for criminals.
Tous les jeunes cités dans l’article por: All the young people quoted in the article have been given pseudonyms, and some contextual details have been changed to protect their anonymity and ensure their safety.
Pour mettre leurs témoignages en perspec: To put their accounts in perspective, I also interviewed several front-line workers who deal every day with young people exposed to these dynamics. I also spoke with criminologist Francesco Carlo Campisi, a postdoctoral researcher, to better understand the mechanisms that shape this kind of recruitment on digital platforms and social media.
<strong>Des adolescents payés pour brûle: Teenagers paid to burn down businesses, rob seniors or shoot at rivals. In Greater Montréal, criminal networks are handing more and more “jobs” to young people, sometimes even minors. In 2024, the phenomenon came into the spotlight with the death of Mohamed-Yanis Seghouani, a 14-year-old killed in Beauce during an attack on a site linked to the Hells Angels.
Un soir de décembre, dans un quartier mo: An evening in December, in a Montréal neighbourhood. The biting cold has emptied the streets, and snow is beginning to pile up on the sidewalks. Inside the premises of a community organization, the atmosphere is very different. The lighting is soft, quiet music plays in the background, and young people are seated around a table. They play cards, trade silly jokes, laugh loudly. At times they perk up their ears when Édouard*, a front-line worker and co-founder of an organization* that serves these young people, reminds them of a rule or starts a more serious conversation.
C’est ici que quatre jeunes ont accepté: It is here that four young people agreed to talk about criminal contracts. One after another, seated on a couch, they tell what they were offered, what they saw, what they did – or refused to do. Behind the door, the laughter goes on. Two worlds coexist under one roof.
Adam is the first to speak. His tone is calm, direct. He makes no attempt to justify himself or play down the facts. “I was recruited for a ‘barbecue’ downtown.” The word is jarring. Adam explains plainly: “A barbecue is when you burn something, when you set a car on fire.” He pauses, then continues: “And I accepted… unfortunately.”
Il rapporte les chiffres platement : « J: He recites the numbers flatly: “I got $1,500. My recruiter got $1,600,” he says, admitting that the gap is absurd. “He’s the one who recruited. That’s how it works in that world.” The regret comes when he thinks about the consequences of what he did. “When I realized that the car I burned could have been mine or my family’s… I regretted it enormously.” His voice trembles slightly.
Derrière la porte, Édouard veille sur le: Behind the door, Édouard keeps an eye on the group. “It’s become so accessible that young people now know the rates,” he warns, off to the side.
In that world, word travels fast. Car theft, barbecue, fraud – every action has its price, adjusted
au risque. Édouard explique que les jeun: to the risk. Édouard explains that young people sometimes show him exchanges on the Telegram app, in closed groups where offers circulate. “They ask me: ‘Do you think I should do it?’”
Les conséquences, Édouard en est témoin: Édouard sees the consequences every day: accidents during police chases, <l1>serious burns like Ali’s,</l1> and sometimes death, like<l2> the terrible end of young Mohamed-Yanis Seghouani</l2>.
<strong>Léo, 18 ans : le choc du drame é: Léo, 18: the shock of a tragedy avoided
Léo est arrivé au Canada il y a deux ans: Léo arrived in Canada two years ago. At school, on the street or on his screen, he says he has never been approached for a contract. But his closest friend almost went down that path, he confides.
Pour 500 $, ce dernier devait participer: For $500, his friend was supposed to take part in a break-in at a house. “It was supposed to be his
première fois, précise Léo. Mais le jour: first time,” Léo says. “But on the day of the job, he felt uneasy.” So he backed out and stood up his recruiters. The next day, he learned the operation had ended badly. Léo lowers his voice when he talks about it. His friend found out what had happened and understood what he had escaped. The shock was immediate. He stopped sleeping, needed to talk, and called Léo.
Pour ce dernier aussi, quelque chose se: For Léo too, something cracked at that moment. The realization was brutal. “He got scared. He’s still in shock,” Léo adds about his friend. His friend has “completely changed” since that day. His life has reorganized itself around simple anchors: home, school, family. “He changed his mentality. Good for him,” Léo believes.
Manu est né au Québec. Il a passé plusie: Manu was born in Quebec. He spent several years of his childhood in his parents’ home country before coming back to the country of his birth. He, too, was approached. “They offered me to burn down a house,” he says in a measured tone. The offer is clear, and so is the sum: $5,000. He doesn’t hesitate for long. “I knew it would end badly.”
Le recruteur n’est pas un inconnu. « C’e: The recruiter is no stranger. “He’s a friend of mine who already does this. He would tell me what went on with the guys who did it, how it is and everything.” One day, they were short on hands; the “friend” turned to Manu and offered him a contract. Manu thought of his parents and turned the offer down without hesitation. “They worked so that I could be here. I couldn’t do that.”
Le jeune montréalais compare sa situatio: The young Montrealer compares his situation with that of others. “They do this with 14-year-olds
pour 500 $, et ces derniers sont impress: for $500, and they’re impressed,” he says. Manu says he saw the trap. “I’d rather work 12 hours a day,” he says, “and earn clean money than hurt people and take a risky path.”
Étudiant au cégep, Yanis parle avec le r: A CEGEP student, Yanis speaks with the distance of someone who has never carried out a contract but knows the network from the inside. “30% of the people I know are involved. 70% want to get in,” says the teenager, who estimates he has about 200 friends and acquaintances. His eyes light up as he describes an ecosystem that is informal, yes, but structured. “I know people who take part in serious crimes,” he says. About four months ago, the members of a family in Saint-Léonard were woken in the middle of the night because their car was on fire in front of their house. The fire was no accident, according to Yanis. “It was payback,” he says. The target wasn’t the vehicle but the family’s youngest daughter.
Le « barbecue » a été exécuté par deux a: The “barbecue” was carried out by two teenagers from the neighbourhood, recruited for the occasion, but it was ordered, he continues, by an older man known for his illegal activities. Yanis knows both sides of the story. The victim and the man who ordered the job used to be a couple. “When you have money, you have
pouvoir », résume-t-il. Après la rupture: power,” he sums up. After the breakup, the man allegedly paid minors to burn his ex’s parents’ car, simply to get revenge.
Le mode opératoire, le jeune collégien l: The young CEGEP student describes the method plainly: teenagers go to a
station-service, remplissent discrètemen: gas station, discreetly fill a jerrycan with gasoline, then come back at night. “They put the gas all around the car, inside it, everywhere. Then they set it on fire,” Yanis says. According to him, the young woman allegedly recognized her ex on neighbourhood surveillance cameras, but fear was stronger. “She was so afraid of him that she said she didn’t know him,” says the young CEGEP student.
Yanis affirme se démarquer de ce milieu,: Yanis says he sets himself apart from that world, even though he knows it from the inside. He watches the phenomenon with sadness and distance, never presenting himself as someone who lectures others. When a crime happens in Montréal, he says, young people are often the first to know. An informal, nocturnal circulation of information allows details to be shared quickly, including the identity of those responsible, long before police investigations make any headway.
« Quand il y a un crime à Montréal, n’im: “When there’s a crime in Montréal, anything at all, it takes three, four or five days of investigation to find out who did it. We already know,” he says.
Quand on lui demande à quelle fréquence: Asked how often he sees young people being approached for criminal contracts, Édouard answers without hesitation: “All the time.” Since the pandemic, he observes, the phenomenon has accelerated and changed. “We’re starting to see a lot of offers in closed groups online. But there are also recruiters in schools, in parks, not to mention word of mouth…”
Pour lui, parler d’une simple « offre »: For him, calling it a simple “offer” is reductive. “It’s not just making a proposal to a young person. It’s an investment.” Before any concrete request, he explains, the target is observed, assessed, prepared. “They measure his vulnerability. Does the kid need money? Does he have a safety net? A parent who’s around, an older brother?” Once the profile is established, recruiters wait for the right moment: “Parents separating, bullying, dropping out of school. They choose the right moment and the right person. They invest in vulnerability.”
Une fois dans le circuit, la jeune recru: Once in the circuit, the young recruit will follow a trajectory, explains Ismaël Benyettou, a psychosocial worker at the Centre de loisirs communautaire de Saint-Michel. “The word ‘recruitment’ gives the impression of something sudden, almost spectacular. In reality, it’s gradual, relational. It fits into paths marked by unmet needs and a context of social exclusion.”
Ismaël Benyettou, intervenant psychosoci: Ismaël Benyettou, psychosocial worker at the Centre de loisirs communautaire de Saint-Michel. Photo credit: Nouri Nesrouche
Formé en psychoéducation et en criminolo: Trained in psychoeducation and clinical criminology, he sees behind these acts “repeated trauma, along with difficulties in emotional regulation, planning and anticipating consequences.” Factors that, combined, “create fertile ground for slipping.”
Dans ce processus, l’argent agit comme u: In this process, money acts as a powerful accelerator. “Young people present it as something very simple, risk-free,” Édouard says. “They tell themselves that at worst, they’ll end up in a youth centre.” The amounts speak for themselves. “Imagine: $1,000 for half an hour. For a 14- or 15-year-old, that’s huge,” he points out.
Beverly Jacques, intervenant jeunesse et: Beverly Jacques, a youth worker and founder of DOD Basketball in Saint-Léonard, sees the same effect. “Money has become a vital need. It’s been associated with freedom, with power. When a young person can do in a few days what their parents do in a year, it completely upends their bearings.”
Antoine Riguerre, agent de mobilisation: Antoine Riguerre, a mobilization officer at Équipe RDP, also sees the influence of social media. “Young people are caught up in this ideology of ‘I’m in America, I want the big house, the big car, my place in the sun.’ When school or work don’t seem like fast tracks to those goals, they take as role models the people who flaunt their success online.”
À court terme, reconnaît Ismaël Benyetto: In the short term, Ismaël Benyettou acknowledges, the system works. “The young person has money, status, recognition, sometimes a substitute family.”
Ce dernier décrit aussi des lieux de rep: He also describes refuges that are an integral part of this world. “They call it the bando or the trap.” These are, he explains, places where the group gets together. Often they are illegally rented apartments, sometimes Airbnbs. For these young people from disadvantaged backgrounds, these spaces offer protection, recognition and a sense of belonging all at once, a form of security their life path has not always given them.
Les réseaux sociaux sont devenus les nou: Social media have become the new back alleys where criminal “jobs” for teenagers are arranged. Beverly Jacques speaks of a territory that adults still look at too little. “We always talk about the physical neighbourhood. But there’s also the digital neighbourhood. If you’re not plugged in, you miss part of young people’s lives.”
Selon lui, les adolescents « vivent troi: According to him, teenagers “live three lives”: personal, school and digital. “During COVID, they built themselves a world. That’s where a lot of problems grew,” he explains, citing the platforms Snapchat, Telegram, Discord and Instagram.
Si le recrutement sur le terrain reste c: While recruitment on the ground remains central, digital tools have profoundly changed the dynamic. “Before, gangs tagged walls. Today, they tag social media,” sums up Francesco Campisi, a researcher in criminology and the sociology of digital technology at Simon Fraser University.
Ce phénomène, qu’il qualifie de « cyberb: This phenomenon, which he calls “cyberbanging,” rests on a constant online presence. “The platforms work like storefronts. They give social capital: respect, power, protection.” Most social media content is not explicitly criminal. “You see sports, music, cars. But about 85% of gang-related content is propaganda: money, weapons, symbols, lifestyle. Like influencer marketing. They sell a way of life, not a product.”
Mais ce territoire numérique n’est pas q: But this digital territory is not just a space for observation or analysis. Édouard sees it driving decisions, movements, actions. “They show me the exchanges, the screenshots, groups on Telegram known for sharing contract offers,” he says.
Édouard distingue toutefois les offres a: Édouard does, however, distinguish between the anonymous offers that circulate online and targeted recruitment, often more discreet, that happens in schools or close circles. When these situations involve minors who are in school, he often runs up against what he calls institutional denial: “Schools say: ‘That doesn’t happen here, it happens outside.’”
Pourtant, affirme-t-il, les jeunes nomme: Yet, he says, the young people themselves name the places and the people. “They tell me: ‘Someone at school approached me and said, “Do you want to make money?”’”
Ce décalage entre le terrain et les inst: This gap between the ground and the institutions deeply concerns him. “We know
comment ça fonctionne. Mais comment ça s: how it works. So how come schools and the authorities say they don’t know?”
Dans le local, les jeunes ont repris leu: In the room, the young people have gone back to their card game, the music comes back up, and so does the laughter. Édouard puts away a few chairs and keeps an eye on the group without stepping in. Adam is still there. He listens to the others, a half-smile on his face. Four years ago, his mother noticed a change in his habits. She then turned to the organization for help, and little by little, Adam found his footing again. “Today, I’m finishing high school. I’m no longer on that bad path,” he says proudly in the privacy of the office.
Sous ce même toit, on tente de combler c: Under this same roof, they try to fill in what the system leaves undone: time, a constant presence, a bond that doesn’t break at the first misstep. Sometimes, that bond keeps everything from falling apart. Sometimes, it simply means not being alone.
